prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level and opening laboratory tests of relativity and fundamental constants

statement.case_for: My view of the science has not moved, but the chair's question about what the lattice clock has taught us deserves a direct answer, because it is the real dividing line. The magic-wavelength idea is a statement of atomic structure: for a chosen wavelength the dynamic polarisabilities of the two clock levels are equal, so the trap light does not move the transition, and confinement in the Lamb-Dicke regime removes Doppler and recoil shifts. That is a quantitative prediction that nature then confirmed, in Katori's group first and then elsewhere. What the lattice added to the older single-ion clocks is a very large number of atoms measured simultaneously, which gives stability that ions cannot reach and, with Ye's group, control of lattice-induced and atom-atom interaction shifts down to about 1e-18. What the community has learned with it is concrete: a gravitational redshift resolved over about a millimetre, which is the relativistic effect seen in a laboratory sample; improved limits on drift of fundamental constants and on coupling to dark matter; and the observation that interactions between fermionic atoms must be understood as a many-body problem even in a clock. No deviation from known physics has been found, as Danielsson rightly says, but a null result at this level is a new measurement of nature, and so is the confirmation of the redshift. The evidence is also what I trust most: Sr, Yb and Hg clocks in several continents agree in frequency ratios, so no single group's modelling carries the result. In the committee I am the member who has spent years computing the level shifts that these experiments have to control, and that is exactly why I think the case is mature. I would draft the citation around the lattice clock and not around precision in general, so that it reads as a distinct invention and not as a third clock prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains framing: a sceptic may call this an outstanding instrument and not a discovery, and I cannot rule out that the committee agrees. I have also weighed whether the pending redefinition of the second should be awaited. I do not think it should, because the physics and the inter-laboratory agreement already exist and a redefinition is a decision by metrologists, not a scientific condition; but I accept that Kroll and Mehlig read it differently. On credit, two names cannot represent PTB, SYRTE, Takamoto, Lemonde, Lisdat and others, and I cannot verify from memory the exact dates of the first strontium lattice spectroscopy or of the first 1e-18 evaluation. If the record shows an earlier decisive demonstration by someone outside the pair, the configuration would have to be revisited. Finally, my taste for theory-experiment agreement is not a criterion, and the B032 case is a serious one that I am poorly placed to judge.

responses.point: Olsson argued that adding a third lattice-clock name would dilute a credit that is clean with two, and that the committee should hold at Katori and Ye unless the historical record shows an earlier original experiment by someone else.
responses.response: I was persuaded. In round 1 I left a third name open because several groups made decisive contributions, but the Nobel prize does not have to enumerate every contributor, and no obvious third name stands out: the proposal and first Sr lattice work belong to Katori, and the demonstration of 1e-18 with controlled many-body shifts belongs to Ye. I now propose exactly two names and I attach one condition, the same one you give, that the expert record on first realisation be checked before the citation is final. If that check turns up an earlier original experiment, I will say so at the vote.

responses.point: Kroll wants the citation to say optical lattice clocks and not precision clocks in general, and he worries about overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
responses.response: We agree on the wording and I have changed my citation to follow it: the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, with neutral atoms at a magic wavelength. On the maturity argument I now go further than in round 1. You treat precision as the achievement; I think the better framing is what the precision exposed, the millimetre redshift, the constant and dark-matter bounds, and the many-body shifts in the lattice. That is the sentence that makes it a physics prize for members who ranked it seventh. I do not share your concern that the pending redefinition of the second should be a condition for completeness.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers topological insulators because band topology replaced symmetry breaking as the organising principle, and he ranked the lattice clock seventh, calling it the most broadly supported candidate but doubting that it is distinct from 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: Your reply to the chair is useful, because you say that B041 is the most broadly supported candidate and you put it among your alternatives, so I read your seventh rank as an overlap objection and not a scientific one. On overlap: the 2005 prize honoured the comb as a way of counting optical cycles, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems. The lattice clock is neither; its new element is cancelling the trap shift so that many neutral atoms can be confined and read out together. I also take your point that credit in B032 is incomplete whichever trio is chosen, and as a non-expert in condensed matter I cannot resolve whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are decisive. That uncertainty is the reason I keep B032 as my first alternative and do not argue against it on science.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers a prediction confirmed by nature, accepts that no deviation from known physics has yet been seen with lattice clocks, and could live with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp while asking for an explicit decision on Mele versus Hasan.
responses.response: I accept that a discovery in your sense, a prediction found in a material, is the cleanest kind, and I think the magic-wavelength condition qualifies in a modest way, since it is a predicted cancellation that was verified. The null result on constants and dark matter is real information and I would not call it a failure. On your Mele versus Hasan question I will say what I can, which is limited: it is a condensed-matter judgement. I note that you and Eriksson both treat the 2D quantum spin Hall state as the secure core, and a citation tied to that core would avoid the 3D ARPES priority dispute. That would make B032 a clean fallback for me, and I would vote for it with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp if the B041 case failed.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers Kane, Mele and Molenkamp for the quantum spin Hall state and says that the agreement of measured spectra with first-principles electronic structure is the kind of link he trusts, while granting that B046 or B041 are cleaner on attribution.
responses.response: That last sentence matters to me. We value the same thing: a result in which measurement and calculation agree quantitatively, in your case ARPES and band theory and in mine frequency ratios and atomic structure. By that criterion the two candidates are on a similar footing, and the difference is the concept at stake, band topology against a measurement regime. The chair asks which criterion should weigh more when attribution and novelty point in different directions. For me, attribution cleanliness is not a substitute for scientific judgement, but a prize that is hard to defend on names damages the physics it honours, and I would put that weight on the clock side.

uncertainties: Whether the expert record confirms that Katori's group made the first strontium lattice clock and magic-wavelength spectroscopy and that Ye's group produced the first 1e-18 evaluation; I rely on general knowledge and have not checked priority claims or the uncertainty values.

Whether the committee will read the lattice clock as a discovery that tests relativity and constants or as an instrument and metrology achievement, and whether three members who ranked it seventh hold a scientific or only an overlap objection.
Whether Ye's contribution to frequency combs makes any part of the credit look like a repeat of 2005, which I address through wording and not through a change of names.
For B032 I cannot judge the HgTe and 3D credit chain, and for B038 I cannot weigh the Cirac, Zoller and Jaksch theory credit against Bloch and Greiner.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori or Ye: my collaborators (Anne L'Huillier, 2023 laureate, the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, Dahlström, Argenti, Schuch, Indelicato) do not overlap with them. I note as before that my field, atomic physics, is close to B041 and that I computed level shifts and structure for storage-ring and attosecond work, which may bias me towards it. The mild user relationship with X-ray free-electron laser sources (B005) is unchanged and B005 is not in my configuration. I have no disclosure beyond this, and I do not think any recusal is needed. I note the chair's question on Johansson's proximity to B031 and defer to the committee, as I have no tie to B031.
